newsitem.title: USA: Social Security Administration shuts down Web site.
newsitem.headline: Social Security Administration shuts down Web site.

text.p: The Social Security Administration Wednesday shut down a controversial Internet Web site, responding to concerns that sensitive financial records of millions of Americans may have been put at risk.

Acting Social Security Commissioner John Callahan told reporters he was temporarily suspending the service while the agency carried out a rigorous evaluation to ensure there were sufficient safeguards to protect confidential data.

The agency will hold public meetings over the next 60 days to evaluate the recently launched service, which allows individuals to look up earnings and benefit estimate statements after entering a few key bits of personal data.

"Nothing is more important to Social Security than maintaining the public's confidence in our ability to carry out one of the primary missions of protecting the privacy of ... sensitive data," Callahan said. "That confidence has been called into question."
Callahan said there had been no reports of fraud under the new service. Responding to news reports about possible security problems, however, top lawmakers had asked the agency to suspend operation.

"I am gratified by the prompt action of the Social Security Administration," said Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican. "I believe this action shows a keen sensitivity to the important privacy concerns shared by most Americans.
The SSA last month began offering the service to make it easier for people to access their financial records and plan for retirement.
Using a name, Social Security number, mother's maiden name, birthdate and place of birth, an individual can look up decades of past earnings records and projected Social Security benefits.
Some privacy experts have said it may be too easy for scam artists or nosy friends and relatives to gain access to the confidential information.
In the past, people wanting such information had to go to a local Social Security office or write to the agency -- a practice they must return to while the site is shut down.

"I hope there are ways in which the SSA can work with security and privacy experts to deal with this in a simple, cost effective manner.... unfortunately, I think they didn't think through all the privacy implications," said Deirdre Mulligan of the Centre for Democracy and Technology.
Callahan said the SSA built in a number of safeguards and was confident the data was secure, but neverthless wanted a thorough review. The Web site address was http://www.ssa.gov.

Republican and Democratic Senate leaders had asked Callahan to halt the service until the SSA convened an independent panel of computer and privacy experts to recommend additional safeguards to ensure confidentiality.
Republican Leader Trent Lott and Democratic Leader Tom Daschle signed a letter calling for suspension, which was sponsored by Roth and ranking Democrat Daniel Patrick Moynihan of New York.
In the House, Pennsylvania Democratic Representative Paul Kanjorski planned to introduce a bill to bar the agency from posting earnings and benefit estimate statements on the Web site.
Kentucky Republican Representative Jim Bunning, chairman of the House Ways and Means subcommittee that oversees the SSA, also asked for a thorough review of the service.
"While I appreciate SSA's desire to provide fast and expedient service, such action should not compromise the privacy of Americans," Bunning said.

The Web site had been getting about 3,000 queries a day since it was made available about a month ago. It got 85,000 on Tuesday, probably due in part to a spate of news reports about the site and possible privacy concerns.
In fact, some people who tried to look at their records were unable to gain access because so many people are trying to view the site.
